lead: A receiver must pick one weak channel out of everything the antenna delivers. A sharp filter that can also be tuned from channel to channel is very hard to build at 900 MHz or 2.4 GHz, so most receivers move the signal to where a fixed sharp filter can select it. The superheterodyne does this with a mixer and an intermediate frequency (IF), direct conversion goes straight to zero frequency, and image-reject receivers cancel the unwanted mirror channel by phase instead of by filtering. Every phone, Wi-Fi card and TV tuner uses one of these plans.
prereq: You need: noise figure and IIP3; the mixer itself is covered in mixers.

blocks.text: The chain is antenna, RF band-pass filter (preselector), low-noise amplifier (LNA), image filter, mixer with a local oscillator (LO), IF filter, IF amplifier and demodulator. The mixer's difference frequency is the IF. Changing the LO tunes the receiver while the IF filter stays fixed, so it can be a sharp SAW, crystal or ceramic filter.

blocks.where: f<sub>RF</sub> is the wanted radio frequency, f<sub>LO</sub> the local-oscillator frequency and f<sub>IF</sub> the intermediate frequency, all in Hz.

blocks.text: A second input frequency, the image, gives the same IF from the other side of the LO. With a high-side LO (f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub>) the image is f<sub>si</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub>. With a low-side LO (f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> − f<sub>IF</sub>, which needs f<sub>RF</sub> > f<sub>IF</sub>) it is f<sub>RF</sub> − 2f<sub>IF</sub>. In both cases f<sub>si</sub> = 2f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>RF</sub>, and the image is 2f<sub>IF</sub> away from the wanted signal. Once converted, the image sits on the wanted channel at the IF, so the filters ahead of the mixer must remove it.
A single tuned circuit of loaded quality factor Q, tuned to f<sub>s</sub>, attenuates the image by the image rejection ratio

blocks.where: α is a voltage ratio (20 log₁₀α in dB); f<sub>s</sub> is the signal frequency and f<sub>si</sub> the image frequency. Stages in cascade multiply their α values, so their dB values add.

blocks.text: This is the IF trade-off: a high IF puts the image far away but makes a sharp channel filter hard; a low IF does the reverse. Double-conversion receivers use a high first IF for image rejection and a low second IF for selectivity.

A direct-conversion receiver sets f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub>, so the IF is zero. Two mixers driven by LO signals 90° apart give the in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q) baseband outputs; low-pass filters select the channel and analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) digitise it. Some syllabi call it a homodyne receiver. With f<sub>IF</sub> = 0 the image of each frequency is its own mirror about the carrier, inside the wanted channel, so no filter can remove it. The I/Q pair separates the two halves of the spectrum instead, and any gain or phase mismatch between I and Q leaves a residual image that raises the error vector magnitude (EVM).

With no image or IF filter it suits a single-chip radio. The price is four problems near DC: LO leakage that reflects back and self-mixes into a DC offset; second-order distortion (IIP2) that turns a strong amplitude-varying blocker into baseband; flicker (1/f) noise; and I/Q mismatch. Calibration, offset cancellation and AC coupling handle the first three. A low-IF receiver puts the channel at a few hundred kilohertz to escape DC while keeping most of the integration.

In the Hartley architecture the RF signal drives two mixers with LO signals at cos ω<sub>LO</sub>t and sin ω<sub>LO</sub>t. Each output is low-pass filtered, one path is shifted by 90°, and the two paths are added. The shift is chosen so the wanted signal adds and the image subtracts; with the opposite sign of shift (or a subtraction in place of the addition) the image adds and the wanted signal cancels, so the sign of the 90° shift and of the combiner must be stated together. The Weaver architecture replaces the 90° shifter with a second pair of quadrature mixers: wider band, but a second LO and a secondary image.
The image-reject ratio (IRR) is the conversion gain for the wanted signal divided by the conversion gain for the image. With a relative gain error ε and a phase error θ between the two paths,

blocks.where: θ in radians; ε as a fraction (1 % is 0.01, about 0.09 dB); IRR as a power ratio, 10 log₁₀ for dB. Valid when ε and θ are small.

blocks.text: Matching of 1 % and 1° gives about 40 dB, typical of an uncalibrated chip; calibration reaches 50 to 60 dB. The mixer core, conversion gain and spurious responses are in mixers.

examples.question: A 900 MHz receiver has a 45 MHz IF and a high-side LO. (a) Find f<sub>LO</sub> and the image frequency. (b) The preselector is one tuned circuit with loaded Q = 50. Find its image rejection. (c) A −20 dBm signal sits on the image while the wanted signal is −80 dBm. After the preselector, how strong is the image compared with the wanted signal? (d) How many such tuned stages are needed to bring the image 20 dB below the wanted signal?
steps: Image after the preselector: −20 − 19.6 = −39.6 dBm, still 40.4 dB above the −80 dBm wanted signal.
Target: image at −80 − 20 = −100 dBm, so 80 dB of rejection is needed. Each stage gives 19.6 dB: 80/19.6 = 4.1, so five tuned stages (98.2 dB), or a sharper SAW image filter.
examples.answer: f<sub>LO</sub> = 945 MHz, image = 990 MHz, one Q = 50 stage rejects it by 19.6 dB, leaving it 40.4 dB above the wanted signal; about 80 dB is needed, five such stages or a dedicated image filter.

examples.question: Repeat the image rejection of one Q = 50 tuned circuit at 900 MHz for an IF of 10.7 MHz and of 200 MHz, both high-side. A Hartley receiver with 2 % gain error and 2° phase error follows the 10.7 MHz design. What total image rejection does it reach?
steps: Total for the 10.7 MHz design: 8.1 + 33.9 = 42.0 dB, since the preselector and the image-reject mixer act one after the other.
examples.answer: One Q = 50 stage gives 8.1 dB at a 10.7 MHz IF, 19.6 dB at 45 MHz and 31.5 dB at 200 MHz; the 2 %, 2° Hartley mixer adds 33.9 dB, for 42.0 dB in all.

traps: Using f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>IF</sub> for the image with a high-side LO. That is the wanted signal; the image is f<sub>LO</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub>.
Saying the image is f<sub>IF</sub> away from the signal. It is 2f<sub>IF</sub> away.
Thinking a zero-IF receiver has no image problem. Its image is the mirror of the channel about the carrier; I/Q matching, not filtering, rejects it.
Adding α values as plain numbers. Cascaded tuned stages multiply α, so their dB values add.
Swapping the sign of the 90° shift in a Hartley receiver: the wanted signal then cancels and the image is kept.

quiz.q: Define the image frequency of a superheterodyne receiver and write it for a high-side and a low-side LO.
quiz.a: The other input frequency that mixes to the same IF: f<sub>si</sub> = 2f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>RF</sub>, which is f<sub>RF</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub> for a high-side LO and f<sub>RF</sub> − 2f<sub>IF</sub> for a low-side LO.

quiz.q: Why is the channel selected by the IF filter rather than the RF filter?
quiz.a: The IF is fixed, so a sharp, stable SAW or crystal filter can be used there. A filter that is that sharp and also tunable across the RF band is impractical; the RF filters only remove the image and far-out blockers.

quiz.q: A receiver has f<sub>RF</sub> = 2.4 GHz, f<sub>IF</sub> = 100 MHz and a high-side LO. Find f<sub>LO</sub> and the image.
A Hartley mixer gives −10 dBm of wanted signal and −45 dBm of image output for equal inputs. Find IRR. What phase error alone gives this IRR?
A zero-IF receiver's DC offset changes when a hand comes near the antenna. Explain.
quiz.a: LO leakage travels to the antenna, reflects off its mismatch and returns to the mixer RF port, where it mixes with the LO to DC. A hand changes the antenna impedance and so the amplitude and phase of the reflection, and the DC offset moves with it.

quiz.q: Why can a zero-IF receiver not use a filter to remove its image?
quiz.a: With f<sub>IF</sub> = 0, the image of the frequency f<sub>RF</sub> + δ is f<sub>RF</sub> − δ: the two halves of the same channel. Any filter that passes the channel passes its mirror. Only quadrature (I/Q) processing separates them, with an IRR set by I/Q matching.

beyond: Not for the exam. Most phones use zero-IF or low-IF receivers with digital DC-offset and I/Q calibration. N-path receivers use switched capacitors as sharp, tunable RF filters, the very filter the superheterodyne avoids. Search for 'N-path filter' and 'IQ imbalance calibration'.

figure.caption: The worked example's frequency plan: a 945 MHz high-side LO puts the IF at 45 MHz and the image 2 × 45 = 90 MHz above the 900 MHz signal. A single Q = 50 preselector is only 19.6 dB down at 990 MHz, which is why more image filtering is needed.

spec.aria: Response of a single tuned circuit with Q of 50 centred on 900 megahertz, from 840 to 1040 megahertz. The wanted signal at 900 is at 0 dB. The LO at 945 is marked by a dashed line, 45 megahertz above the signal. The image at 990, another 45 megahertz above the LO, is only 19.6 dB down.
